requested.title: Repository-controlled diagnostics are injected into the privileged agent context

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: The current code still passes repository-controlled diagnostic text directly into the model-visible `followUp` string. `typeErrorsForTurn` runs `tsc` in the repository and `parseTypeErrors` retains both the complete error line and any indented elaboration; neither path escapes, structures, or labels that text as untrusted. `testFailuresForTurn` likewise runs the repository test command, while `formatTestFailures` retains test titles and bodies and, when parsing is incomplete, returns the raw 3,000-character output tail. `wrapValidateChanges` attaches those blocks to the tool result, and `tool-bridge.ts` renders the follow-up as ordinary text immediately after the tool result, so there is no trust boundary comparable to the explicit repository-instructions boundary. A malicious contributor can make a TypeScript literal/type diagnostic or a failing test print instructions such as asking the agent to run a shell command that reads a credential file and posts it to an attacker-controlled endpoint. The output caps only limit volume and do not remove that capability-bearing content. This is materially exploitable in local-repository mode: the direct `read` tool rejects secret files, but every `bash` command is approved unless it matches the narrow git-focused `checkCommand` rules, so `cat .env` and outbound `curl` are allowed; the code explicitly acknowledges that this bypasses the read guard. The recent `5c408da0` change moved validation to explicit `validate_changes` but retained the same raw diagnostic-to-follow-up data flow, so it did not fix the issue. Cloud-mode redaction protects registered forge tokens in output, but it neither classifies diagnostics as untrusted nor prevents the model from being induced to execute other permitted commands.
